title: Real Latin through the Naibbe cipher, in the manuscript's layout, against every established fact
method: Greshko's published Naibbe cipher run on real Latin, at the pinned revision (greshko/naibbe-cipher@5145f526b52741a6dca14201147f687e62c7162e): naibbe_v2.py with the published 78-card deck, RESPACING=17 and UNAMBIGUOUS=True, Python random seed 0, the first 12,000 words of the pinned Latin reference text (vs.facts.ref_words) encrypted in one call. Ambiguity retries were 0, so this is an exact reversible encryption of the Latin, which I verified separately by decrypting it back with the repository's own decrypt_naibbe.py and getting the plaintext letter for letter. Layout is the manuscript's shape, not the cipher's: eight tokens to a line and seven lines to a paragraph, so the opener share matches the manuscript's own (one paragraph-opening line per seven), and each paragraph's first line is reported separately in first_lines exactly as the scorer takes them. Nothing in the procedure consults position. The table for each token is drawn from a shuffled 78-card deck (create_card_deck) and the deck index walks forward, so a token's form depends only on how many tokens precede it, never on where it stands in a line or a paragraph. That is the whole question of K-006-open-1: the cipher is reversible and locally Voynich-like, but does it produce the positional structure the manuscript has? This run measures it against every established fact rather than against the two statistics the cipher was tuned to match.
